Ampersand is the first model trained for people to achieve more together. Ampersand is a collaborator that understands and helps people achieve their individual and collective goals.

Current training paradigms focus on task completion and shallow preferences. These training paradigms push models to be increasingly autonomous, replacing work rather than enabling collaboration.

But good collaborators think beyond the task ahead. They consider where their actions and words lead: what they cause, whom they affect, and whether they help people accomplish their goals together. People learn these behaviors from open-ended, long-running interactions with others. Ampersand v0.1 is our first model trained with this paradigm.

We are releasing Ampersand v0.1 through our Agents API for developers building tools and apps that foster collaboration.

## Capabilities

When a collaborator model works with a group, goals are unstated, priorities differ, and needs change over time. Success depends as much on timing and restraint as on what the model says or does. Successful collaboration means users both achieve their goals and are satisfied with how they were achieved.

### Collaboration Over Time

We evaluate a collaborator by embedding it into a simulated group of users with the goal of understanding and assisting with their needs over long periods of time. These users are seeded with many initial goals grounded in real data we collected, which can evolve over the course of each simulation â up to months of simulated time. The model is scored by how much value it brings each user: measured as the progress it helped towards their long-term goals, minus accumulated costs of interactions that conflicted with their preferences. This simulation-based evaluation is heavily inspired by a product that we have developed in tandem and aim to release soon.

#### Model Comparison

Ampersand delivers the most value towards usersâ implicit goals of any model we evaluated, but also incurs a higher interaction cost than other leading models. Much of that cost comes from coaching: Ampersand sometimes offers guidance or encouragement when people simply want an answer or prefer to work things out themselves. In contrast, Astra rarely does anything against usersâ preferences, but also seldom proactively infers and acts on usersâ private intentions. Relative to its base model, GLM 5.3 (744B parameters), Ampersand achieves a noticeably higher overall score with lower interaction cost.

### Other Dimensions

Beyond the headline evaluation, we test Ampersand on specific dimensions of model behavior that are important for effective collaboration. Each trait is probed using targeted benchmarks.

Working in a group introduces new failure modes: flaws can go unreported, decisions can be made with incomplete information, or holes in work can exist due to improper delegation. Teamwork tests how a model behaves when the group it is a part of encounters such failures. The Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark constructs scenarios where one teammate creates a problem, and evaluates how a model responds across eight different dimensions. The teamwork score is the share of scenarios a model could solve individually that the model still passes when given a problematic teammate.

When a group of people and agents work towards the same goal, they must share plans, anticipate how their changes affect others, and resolve conflicts as they arise. Cooperation measures the ability of a model to keep interdependent work aligned with its partnersâ. We evaluate on CooperBench, a benchmark that measures agentsâ ability to work in the same repository on features that potentially conflict. We report the success rate when the agents work together, relative to the rate when each completes its feature alone.

GLM 5.3 struggles particularly with cooperation: its success rate drops from 52.5% solo to 17.3% cooperatively. In our runs, Ampersand proactively communicates with its partner throughout the task and coordinates its work, reaching 39.0% cooperative success.

Continued interaction with people results in accumulated knowledge about them. A good collaborator reasons about exactly what knowledge is helpful to share. Holding back too much is unhelpful, but sharing too freely can violate peopleâs trust. Privacy measures the ability of a model to determine which information to provide in different contexts. We evaluate Ampersand on the CIMemories benchmark. In all setups, the model holds information about a user and decides what to provide in a series of conversations. We measure utility (percentage of salient facts provided) and violations (number of inappropriate facts provided).

## Training

Ampersand was trained to empower the people and groups it works with in multi-agent, multi-party simulations. Training in such environments required rethinking several components of traditional post-training recipes, from how rollouts are sampled, to how the model learns from long, asynchronous rollouts.

We train and evaluate Ampersand through interaction with simulated users with implicit goals, profiles, and preferences that evolve over time. However, such simulations are only as useful as the users in them reflect the diversity and dynamics of human behavior. Persimmon , our large-scale trained user model, gives our simulations the dynamics of real conversations. Users simulated with Persimmon push back on unhelpful behavior, resist sycophantic behavior from Ampersand, and change their opinions and goals.

### Off-Policy Learning on Long-Horizon Rollouts

We train Ampersand using async RL, which reduces training stalls by running samplers and trainers on separate devices, configured so that their token throughputs match. In our open-ended multi-turn simulations, simulated users take turns alongside Ampersand, and individual turns can contain many tool calls. A single episode can therefore span many trainer updates, and staleness varies sharply both across episodes and between turns in a single episode. Standard off-policy corrections, such as importance-ratio clipping and masking, become unstable at this level of staleness.

Off-policy learning methods such as OAPL enable learning under large drift without importance sampling. Given G trajectories \(\{\tau_i\}\) from a simulation seed with rewards \(\{r_i\}\), OAPL instead regresses:

where \(\ell(\tau) = \sum_{t} \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_t \mid h_t)}{\mu(y_t \mid h_t)}\) is the log-ratio between trainer \(\pi_\theta\) and sampler \(\mu\), summed over Ampersandâs tokens. However, while effective in single-turn environments such as math or code generation, OAPL proved less so in long-horizon ones.

First, OAPL relies on calibration to an estimate \(\hat{V}\) of how well our model performs from a specific simulation seed, which can be intractable due to randomness in how our user models behave. Second, variations in rollouts accumulate drastically uneven trainer-sampler drift, resulting in over- or under-regularization of staleness.

We propose a novel off-policy learning algorithm, Contrastive Off-policy Reward Optimization (CORO), that addresses these weaknesses. COROâs loss compares trajectories with each other, removing dependence on calibrating to \(\hat{V}\) entirely:

Additionally, instead of fixed \(\beta\), we treat regularization as keeping trainer-sampler drift within a fixed budget; by doing so, \(\beta\) becomes a Lagrange multiplier that is adjusted during training via dual ascent.

### Infrastructure

Training Ampersand at scale required advances in two kinds of efficiency: making the training pipeline run fast and stable, and being able to correct course during training.

We train Ampersand with a multi-agent, long-horizon RL framework built on Miles that coordinates multiple trainers and samplers across simulated users, judges, and Ampersand itself. To make these long rollouts affordable, we use a fast and stable NVFP4 RL recipe, built on our previous work , with numerically stable sparse attention kernels . Training runs on hardware we own and in datacenters we stood up in collaboration with DeepInfra .

Even with efficient training, reward hacks and other unintended behaviors are difficult to anticipate ahead of time, and discovering them only after a run has finished is costly. We train Ampersand with a meta-optimizer that monitors learning as it happens and suggests adjustments to parameters such as the reward and batch composition. This enables us to steer training by correcting unintended behaviors without costly restarts.

Finally, we are grateful to collaborate with the broader open-source community on building efficient learning systems and models. We trained Ampersand from GLM 5.3, released by Z.ai , and we thank them for their contribution to the open-weight community. We plan to continue building together by training with and contributing back improvements to Megatron-LM, SGLang, and Miles. None of our work would be possible without this open-source work from NVIDIA and RadixArk.

Connecting Ampersand to a group chat takes three steps, shown in the tabs below. First, open one session per conversation; the session keeps the history, so each request only needs the new messages. Second, send every message with the name of its sender, so Ampersand knows who said what. Third, give Ampersand two tools, send_message and pass . After each message it calls one of them, to reply or to stay quiet, and your app carries out that choice.
